hits.name: Bryan Johnson
hits.text:
I lay atop a glacier in Iceland. 

It felt like I could feel the Earth's nervous system beneath me.

It was calm, steady and sturdy.

Mine, in contrast, was volcanic.

Perhaps it was the contrast that made it apparent.

My inner world was turbulent: an eruption of debris and turmoil. I think it was the first time in 14 years that I had actually felt my nervous system.

Out of necessity, out of survival, I had taught myself to numb whatever my nervous system was trying to tell me. Ten years of chronic depression had wrecked my mind and body. Building companies, raising three children, sleeping little, living with unhealthy habits and fighting an existential war over my spirituality had all compounded, and numbing it all was the only way I knew to survive.

What I didn't know was that the numbness had made me dead inside. Dead to the world. Beneath it, my nervous system was on high alert, in a constant state of panic, while my mind worked overtime to keep things moving along. It was not sustainable.

Iceland was my first vacation since I'd started building companies. I had come to see Holuhraun, the eruption from the Bárðarbunga volcano and the largest in Iceland in more than 200 years.

I had recently sold my company, Braintree Venmo, and I was trying to find my way back to some semblance of reality, to the mainland of sanity and stability. I couldn't say why, but going to an active volcano felt like the right decision. 

I wanted to touch the lava, to play with it, to feel it. It was almost as if the eruption was calling me, a mirror of myself, inviting me to inspect what I’d hidden from myself.

As I waited for government approval on our helicopter permit to fly to the volcano, I rode a snowmobile across the glacier for hours. In a remote glacial landscape, I stopped and laid down on the ice. I think it was the first time since I was a teenager that I relaxed.

These past five years pursuing Don't Die have been less about living longer and more about undying: trying to come back from the dead.

The chart above shows my HRV, a window into my nervous system. Low means fight or flight. High means calm. Bringing my nervous system back into any kind of balance has been one of the hardest things I've done. It has been a slow, methodical process of bringing myself back to life.

I’m now back to having the nervous system balance of a 20 year old.

People often tell me that my teaching of health comes from a place of luxury. That I can be healthy because I achieved financial success. I understand that and won’t disagree. 

I would add that the wear and tear took me to a very dark place, and I'm fortunate it didn't bury me. Climbing out has taken as much work as falling in. It makes me wonder whether I ever needed to bury myself in the first place.
hits.draft_en:
Bryan Johnson wrote a long one about lying on a glacier in Iceland and feeling his nervous system for the first time in 14 years.

Years of no sleep, stress and numbing it all had him running on panic. He says getting his body to calm down again was one of the hardest things he's done, and he tracked it with HRV.

You don't need a glacier. Most blokes our age push through stress and call it normal. Sleep, walking, getting outside and some quiet time aren't soft. They're maintenance, same as oiling the machine.

Blueberries and yogurt are one of my regular meals to support my brain and cardiovascular health. 

The research on blueberries is fascinating and keeps giving me reasons to come back to them.

Their blue-purple color comes from anthocyanins, a family of plant compounds that have been studied for their effects on blood vessels, cellular signaling, and cognition.

One trial I find interesting gave adults ages 65–80 a daily wild-blueberry powder equivalent to 178 grams of fresh berries (about one cup). After 12 weeks, the blueberry group had better blood vessel function and performed better on tests memory and executive function than the placebo group. This adds to the evidence that these foods can influence specific aspects of how we function.

For me, the appeal is how easily blueberries fit into something I already enjoy eating. Yogurt contributes protein and calcium, and the berries add fiber and plant compounds that make the meal more interesting nutritionally.

I want to stay curious, learn, and keep doing mentally demanding work. The meals I repeat are one part of how I approach that.

Hold on ✋

How is it that, despite my history of severe inflammatory bowel disease, high cholesterol, and no heart disease, I’ve been recommended statins by a dozen doctors, yet not one has ever mentioned randomized controlled trial data suggesting that the statin repeatedly recommended to me might exacerbate my disease?

In this randomized trial, nearly half of the atorvastatin-treated patients experienced a worsening in disease activity, compared with not a single patient in the placebo group.

Now, I’m not claiming this is the be-all and end-all definitive study on the topic.

🚨But how can you have informed consent without information?

Also keep in mind that where literature is mixed on this topic the incentive bias will always skew towards playing up drug benefits and downplaying risks.

And when a drug is being recommended that could even plausibly worsen a patient’s serious pre-existing disease, shouldn’t that possibility at least enter the conversation?
hits.draft_en:

He has a history of serious bowel disease and has been told to take statins by a dozen doctors. Not one mentioned a trial where nearly half the patients on atorvastatin got worse with that disease, compared with none on placebo.

He's not saying it's the final word. His point is you can't give informed consent without the information.

Whatever pill you're offered, ask: what are the downsides for someone like me? A good doctor won't mind the question.

outsiders.name: Greg Brockman

I helped start OpenAI because I want AGI to be safe and beneficial for people. This post provides transparency that can be the foundation of industry-wide shared safety bars.

Perhaps the most important concept from the post is the following: "AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining."

Towards ensuring that safety keeps pace with general intelligence of pretrained models (as measured by "perplexity"), the post proposes "common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors)."
